## The Scale Problem

Technical documentation exhibits a unique growth characteristic: the corpus
expands monotonically with each research direction, specification, and design
record. Over a multi-year horizon, a project of this scope accumulates
thousands of documents across multiple natural languages, output formats, and
audience levels.

Conventional static-site management breaks down at this scale through several
well-understood failure modes:

- **Link rot**: moved or renamed files leave dangling references
- **Include drift**: shared templates change but individual pages are not
  updated
- **Format inconsistency**: new pages omit required metadata or cross-format
  navigation controls
- **Build-time growth**: sequential rebuilds scale linearly with document count
- **Cross-reference decay**: references between documents become stale without
  centralized validation

The platform described here was designed to make these failure modes
**structurally impossible** rather than depending on human discipline or
manual review processes.

## Architectural Principles

The platform rests on three architectural principles that together enable
management at scale:

### Principle 1: Idempotent Pre-Build Validation

All structural checks (link validity, include presence, path correctness) are
performed before the build step, in a dedicated validation pass. Each check is
idempotent: running it repeatedly on an unchanged corpus produces the same
result. A `check` mode reports issues without modifying files, enabling CI/CD
gating with exit code 1.

### Principle 2: Target-Isolated Parallel Rendering

The document corpus is partitioned into independent render targets. Each
target renders into a physically isolated copy of the entire source tree,
eliminating cross-target contention for shared resources. Outputs are merged
into a unified deployment directory after all targets complete.

### Principle 3: Automatic Structural Healing

Common structural defects (broken relative paths, missing includes, incorrect
file extensions in links) are detected and corrected automatically by a chain
of resolvers. Each resolver addresses one class of defect independently and
can be enabled or disabled without affecting the others.

```{python}
#| label: fig-pipeline
#| fig-cap: "Pre-build, render, and post-render pipeline stages"
dot("""
digraph Pipeline {
    rankdir=LR;
    splines=ortho;
    node [shape=box, style=rounded, fontsize=9];
    edge [fontsize=8];

    subgraph cluster_pre {
        label="Structural validation";
        style=filled;
        fillcolor="#E8F4F8";
        color="#2B7A9E";
        fontsize=10;

        Check [label="Automated resolver chain\n(link validity, path correctness,\ninclude presence)", fillcolor="#FFFFFF", style=filled];
        Gen [label="Dynamic index generation\n(git-history-based listing)", fillcolor="#FFFFFF", style=filled];
        Fix [label="Auto-correction of\ndetectable defects", fillcolor="#FFFFFF", style=filled];

        Check -> Gen -> Fix;
    }

    Render [label="Isolated parallel rendering\n(partitioned by render target)", fillcolor="#FFF4E6", style=filled, fontsize=10, width=2.5];

    subgraph cluster_post {
        label="Post-processing";
        style=filled;
        fillcolor="#E6F0E6";
        color="#3A7D44";
        fontsize=10;

        Extract [label="Extract machine-readable\nformat variants", fillcolor="#FFFFFF", style=filled];
        Index [label="Generate hierarchical\ncross-format index", fillcolor="#FFFFFF", style=filled];
    }

    Fix -> Render;
    Render -> Extract;
    Extract -> Index;
}
""")
```

Each stage is idempotent: running it repeatedly on an unchanged corpus produces
identical output. All fixes are validated before any writes occur, and a
dedicated check mode returns exit code 1 on any unresolved issue.

## Resolver Chain Architecture

The structural validation layer is organised as a sequential chain of
independent resolvers, each handling one class of defect:

```{python}
#| label: fig-resolver-chain
#| fig-cap: "Sequential resolver chain, each stage handling one defect class"
dot("""
digraph ResolverChain {
    rankdir=LR;
    splines=ortho;
    node [shape=box, style=rounded, fontsize=9];
    edge [fontsize=9];

    P [label="Path resolver\\ncorrects relative paths that\\nbroke after file moves", fillcolor="#E8F4F8", style=filled];
    L [label="Link resolver\\ndetects links to files that\\nwere renamed or restructured", fillcolor="#E8F4F8", style=filled];
    I [label="Include resolver\\nensures shared templates are\\npresent in every document", fillcolor="#E8F4F8", style=filled];
    D [label="Link-target resolver\\nconverts source extensions\\nto output extensions", fillcolor="#E8F4F8", style=filled];
    Result [label="Structurally valid corpus", fillcolor="#E8F8E8", style=filled];

    P -> L -> I -> D -> Result;
}
""")
```

Each resolver operates independently, with its own scope configuration
inherited from a three-tier model:

- **Global exclusions**: build artifacts, version-control directories
- **Project-level exclusions**: files excluded from the build pipeline
- **Local exclusions**: per-resolver patterns for special cases

This ensures that the project configuration remains the single source of truth
for exclusions while allowing individual resolvers to tighten scope without
modifying global settings.

## Scaling Properties

The resolver chain operates by scanning file content rather than parsing,
achieving sub-second completion on corpora of several thousand files. The
total cost is linear in aggregate file size with extremely small constants,
independent of the number of render targets or the complexity of the document
graph.

Build time is determined by the number of render targets, not the number of
documents:

```{python}
#| label: fig-scaling
#| fig-cap: "Build time is a function of target count, invariant to document count"
dot("""
digraph BuildScaling {
    rankdir=LR;
    splines=ortho;
    node [shape=box, style=rounded, fontsize=9];
    edge [fontsize=9];

    subgraph cluster_small {
        label="100 documents / 5 targets";
        style=filled;
        fillcolor="#E8F4F8";
        color="#2B7A9E";
        fontsize=10;

        S [label="build time = 5  x  T_render", fillcolor="#FFFFFF", style=filled];
    }

    subgraph cluster_med {
        label="1000 documents / 5 targets";
        style=filled;
        fillcolor="#E6F0E6";
        color="#3A7D44";
        fontsize=10;

        M [label="build time = 5  x  T_render", fillcolor="#FFFFFF", style=filled];
    }

    subgraph cluster_large {
        label="10000 documents / 5 targets";
        style=filled;
        fillcolor="#FFF4E6";
        color="#DAA520";
        fontsize=10;

        L [label="build time = 5  x  T_render", fillcolor="#FFFFFF", style=filled];
    }

    S -> M -> L [style=dashed, color=gray, label="100x document growth / no change in build time"];
}
""")
```

Since each render target operates in a physically isolated copy of the source
tree, targets can be distributed across any number of machines without
architectural changes. A single merge step combines the independently
generated output directories using content-level merging for shared assets
(search indexes, site maps) and union semantics for everything else.

```{python}
#| label: fig-parallel-build
#| fig-cap: "Target isolation enables distribution without architectural change"
dot("""
digraph MachineDist {

        M2 [label="Machine / Container B\nsubset of targets", fillcolor="#E6F0E6", style=filled];
        M3 [label="Machine / Container C\nsubset of targets", fillcolor="#FFF4E6", style=filled];
    }

    M1 -> Merge;
    M2 -> Merge;
    M3 -> Merge;
}
""")
```

## Dynamic Content Generation

Beyond structural validation, the platform generates navigational and
cross-format content at render time based on each document's metadata and the
project configuration:

- **Cross-format links** (PDF, machine-readable text) are generated
  automatically, with the link target resolved from project settings
- **Format variant grouping** consolidates multiple alternatives under a single
  heading, avoiding redundant labels
- **Recent-document listings** are generated from version-control history,
  ensuring the front page always reflects current activity without manual
  updates

```{python}
#| label: fig-format-resolve
#| fig-cap: "Format link resolution follows a deterministic chain from project config to per-document override"
dot("""
digraph FormatResolve {
    rankdir=LR;
    splines=ortho;
    node [shape=box, style=rounded, fontsize=9];
    edge [fontsize=9];

    Proj [label="Project config\n(global switch)", fillcolor="#FFE4E1", style=filled, width=2.2];
    Gen [label="Format variant files\ngenerated at build time", fillcolor="#E8F4F8", style=filled];
    Override [label="Per-document\nvisibility control", fillcolor="#FFF4E6", style=filled];
    Show [label="Format link rendered\nin output", fillcolor="#E8F8E8", style=filled];

    Proj -> Gen [label="enables generation"];
    Gen -> Override [label="variant exists"];
    Override -> Show;
}
""")
```

## CI/CD Integration

The full pipeline is containerised and executed in a continuous-deployment
workflow:

```{python}
#| label: fig-ci-pipeline
#| fig-cap: "CI/CD pipeline: validation, build, post-process, deploy"
dot("""
digraph CIPipeline {
    rankdir=LR;
    splines=ortho;
    node [shape=box, style=rounded, fontsize=9];
    edge [fontsize=8];

    Container [label="Container image\n(reproducible environment)", fillcolor="#E8F4F8", style=filled];
    Validate [label="Structural validation\n(fail-fast on defects)", fillcolor="#FFE4E1", style=filled];
    Build [label="Parallel render +\\noutput merge", fillcolor="#FFF4E6", style=filled];
    Post [label="Extract machine-readable\\nvariants + generate index", fillcolor="#E6F0E6", style=filled];
    Deploy [label="Publish to\\nproduction", fillcolor="#E8F8E8", style=filled];

    Container -> Validate;
    Validate -> Build;
    Build -> Post;
    Post -> Deploy;
}
""")
```

Containerisation ensures environment parity between local development and CI.
All pipeline stages are declared in a single configuration file, making the
workflow self-documenting and reproducible.

## Dual-Parallel Build Architecture

The same partitioning that enables logical parallelism within a machine
extends naturally to physical distribution across machines, with zero
additional coordination.

```{python}
#| label: fig-dual-parallel
#| fig-cap: "Two-level hierarchy: logical parallelism within each unit, physical parallelism across units, unified by recursive merge"
dot("""
digraph DualParallel {
    rankdir=TB;
    splines=ortho;
    node [shape=box, style=rounded, fontsize=9];
    edge [fontsize=8];

    Corpus [label="Document Corpus\nN documents, T targets", fillcolor="#E8F4F8", style=filled, width=2.5];

    subgraph cluster_physical {
        label="Physical Layer: Machine Boundary";
        style=dashed;
        color="#888888";
        fontsize=11;

        subgraph cluster_m1 {
            label="Machine 1";
            style=filled;
            fillcolor="#E8F4F8";
            color="#2B7A9E";
            fontsize=10;
            M1_T1 [label="A", fillcolor="#FFFFFF", style=filled, width=0.5];
            M1_T2 [label="B", fillcolor="#FFFFFF", style=filled, width=0.5];
            M1_T3 [label="C", fillcolor="#FFFFFF", style=filled, width=0.5];
            M1_M [label="\u2193", shape=plaintext];
            M1_T1 -> M1_M; M1_T2 -> M1_M; M1_T3 -> M1_M;
        }

        subgraph cluster_m2 {
            label="Machine 2";
            style=filled;
            fillcolor="#E6F0E6";
            color="#3A7D44";
            fontsize=10;
            M2_T1 [label="D", fillcolor="#FFFFFF", style=filled, width=0.5];
            M2_T2 [label="E", fillcolor="#FFFFFF", style=filled, width=0.5];
            M2_M [label="\u2193", shape=plaintext];
            M2_T1 -> M2_M; M2_T2 -> M2_M;
        }

        subgraph cluster_m3 {
            label="Machine N";
            style=filled;
            fillcolor="#FFF4E6";
            color="#DAA520";
            fontsize=10;
            M3_T1 [label="F", fillcolor="#FFFFFF", style=filled, width=0.5];
            M3_T2 [label="G", fillcolor="#FFFFFF", style=filled, width=0.5];
            M3_T3 [label="H", fillcolor="#FFFFFF", style=filled, width=0.5];
            M3_M [label="\u2193", shape=plaintext];
            M3_T1 -> M3_M; M3_T2 -> M3_M; M3_T3 -> M3_M;
        }
    }

    Merge [label="Global Merge\n(commutative)", fillcolor="#E8F8E8", style=filled, width=2.0];

    Corpus -> M1_T1; Corpus -> M1_T2; Corpus -> M1_T3;
    Corpus -> M2_T1; Corpus -> M2_T2;
    Corpus -> M3_T1; Corpus -> M3_T2; Corpus -> M3_T3;

    M1_M -> Merge; M2_M -> Merge; M3_M -> Merge;
}
""")
```

### Commutative Merge

The merge function that combines outputs is **commutative**: merging in any
order produces the same result. This property eliminates the need for
distributed coordination -- no locks, no consensus, no shared state, no leader
election. Machines can complete in any order, including with partial
failures. If a machine fails, its targets are simply missing from the output;
rerun them and merge again.

Partial outputs to the merge point move through any transport layer -- shared
filesystem, object storage, or CI artifact system -- with the merge function
requiring only that remote output be accessible as a local directory tree.

### Failure Model

The commutative merge guarantee makes the architecture resilient by
construction:

| Failure | Effect | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| Machine fails mid-build | Its targets missing | Rerun on another machine; merge is idempotent |
| Single target fails | Only that target absent | Rebuild only that target; merge accepts partial results |
| Network partition | Cannot upload output | Other machines continue; gap detected at merge time |

### Deployment Topologies

The architecture maps to multiple deployment models by changing only the
target assignment strategy:

- **Single machine**: all targets render with logical parallelism; merge is a
  trivial no-op
- **CI runner pool**: each runner picks a target subset from a build queue,
  uploads artifacts; a final job downloads and merges
- **Dedicated cluster**: fixed target groups per machine, shared filesystem
  eliminates transport overhead
- **Hybrid cloud**: baseline load on fixed infrastructure, burst spills to
  ephemeral cloud instances provisioned on demand

All four topologies use the same build command, the same merge function, and
the same deployment pipeline.

## Comparison with Conventional Approaches

| Concern | Conventional approach | This platform |
|---|---|---|
| Link validation | Manual or external CI checker | Pre-build automated scan, sub-second |
| Include management | Manual copy-paste | Automatic insertion of missing includes |
| Format navigation | Hand-written links per document | Auto-generated from configuration |
| Build scaling | Sequential per document | Target-parallel, O(targets) not O(documents) |
| Cross-reference correctness | Manual upkeep | Automatic extension correction |
| Structural robustness | Relies on author discipline | Automated healing of common defects |
| Agent/machine feed | Separate manual pipeline | Integrated extraction at build time |
| CI quality gate | Sparse or absent | Comprehensive check, exit code 1 |

## Conclusion

The platform demonstrates that static-site management at scale is achievable
through a layered automation architecture combining structural validation with
dual-parallel build execution. The key insight is not any individual tool or
technique but the composition of idempotent passes that collectively guarantee
integrity regardless of corpus size.

The system exhibits:

- **Document-count independence** in build time
- **Target-count linearity** in resource requirements
- **Physical partitionability** for distributed execution
- **Self-healing** for common structural defects
- **Configuration-driven** behaviour with a single source of truth
- **CI-native** integration with pre-build validation and post-render processing
